lesson.title: Capstone: El Puente Reading
lesson.subtitle: One connected Madrid story synthesizing all 9 conversion bridges and key structures

hook.title: Look How Far Across the Bridge You Have Walked
hook.content: Thirty topics ago, you started with el pastel, el café, and lo quiero. Today you command all **9 conversion and sound-shift families** (-ción, -dad, -mente, -ar, -ico, -al, f→h, ct→ch, pl/cl→ll), both verbs for 'to be' (ser vs estar), all three past perspectives (he hablado, hablé/fue, hablaba/era/estaba), the near future (voy a), double object pronouns (me lo, se lo), the personal 'a', saber vs conocer, gustar/encantar, the conditional (-ía), and the opposite-vowel subjunctive!

pattern.title: Reading & Producing Connected Spanish Without Translating Word-by-Word
pattern.content: Notice how all these pieces flow together effortlessly in a real Madrid narrative: *Actualmente vivo en Madrid, una ciudad mágica y hermosa. Conozco a muchos amigos en la universidad central. Ayer confirmé la reservación, fuimos al restaurante y comimos muy bien. ¡Me encanta hablar español!*

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: la confirmación / la tradición, la ciudad / la universidad, perfectamente / exactamente, mágico / central, hecho / noche / lleno, me encanta / me gustaría
exercises.meaning: -tion → -ción (100% feminine), -ty → -dad (100% feminine), feminine adj. + -mente (-ly), -ic → accented -ico & -al → invariable -al, f→h, ct→ch, pl/cl→ll shifts, inverted liking & polite conditional
exercises.explanation: All 9 conversion bridges and core grammatical engines work as one integrated system.

exercises.prompt: In 'Actualmente vivo en Madrid desde hace dos años', why is 'vivo' in the present tense and what does 'actualmente' mean?
options: actualmente means 'currently', and Spanish uses the present tense (vivo) with desde hace for actions that began in the past and continue right now!
actualmente means 'actually', and vivo is past tense
exercises.target_answer: actualmente means 'currently', and Spanish uses the present tense (vivo) with desde hace for actions that began in the past and continue right now!
exercises.meaning: Currently I have lived in Madrid for two years
exercises.explanation: Two signature Spanish rules in one sentence: false friend actualmente ('currently') + present-tense duration with desde hace!

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I love this magical city and I understand what you say'
exercises.target_answer: Me encanta esta ciudad mágica y comprendo lo que dices
exercises.meaning: I love this magical city and I understand what you say
exercises.explanation: Me encanta esta ciudad mágica + y comprendo lo que dices.

exercises.idea: say: 'I have the confirmation and I am going to give it to him today'
cues: I have the confirmation → Tengo la confirmación
and I am going to give it (fem. la!) to him (le → se!) today → y se la voy a dar hoy
idea_parts: I have the confirmation → Tengo la confirmación
and I am going to give it to him today → y se la voy a dar hoy
exercises.target_answer: Tengo la confirmación y se la voy a dar hoy
exercises.meaning: I have the confirmation and I am going to give it to him today
exercises.explanation: Tengo la confirmación y se la voy a dar hoy — combining tener, -ción, se la, and ir a + infinitive!

diagnosis.slip: used se lo instead of se la for la confirmación
diagnosis.cue: Because la confirmación is feminine, 'it' is la: se la voy a dar.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Me gustaría visitar la universidad central mañana
exercises.target_answer: Me gustaría visitar la universidad central mañana
exercises.meaning: I would like to visit the central university tomorrow
cues: to visit the university: visitar la universidad
exercises.explanation: Me gustaría visitar la universidad central mañana.
exercises.affirmation: You just synthesized the conditional, -ar verb, -dad noun, and -al adjective in one breath!

summary.outcome: Synthesize all 9 Spanish conversion bridges and core grammatical structures in connected reading and production.

use_example.german: Me encanta esta ciudad mágica, comprendo perfectamente lo que dices y se lo voy a explicar a mi amigo.
use_example.english: I love this magical city, I understand perfectly what you say, and I am going to explain it to my friend.

summary.takeaway: You don't memorize Spanish — you reconstruct it live from the Latin and structural bridges you already own.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([3001] A Day in Madrid: Reading): read and build a connected narrative through a full day in Madrid.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'Hopefully you have a fantastic day!'

payoff.text: From 'Quiero el pastel' and 'Lo quiero' in Topic 1 to 'Tengo la confirmación y se la voy a dar hoy' in Topic 30 — the bridge is yours!

ciudad.etymology_derivation: Latin cīvitātem ('citizenship, city') gives English 'city' and 'civic', and Spanish ciudad.

universidad.etymology_derivation: Latin universitātem → universidad. English -ty is Spanish -dad, and every -dad noun is feminine.

tradición.etymology_derivation: Latin trāditiō ('a surrender, handing over') — tradition is knowledge handed across generations.

confirmación.etymology_derivation: Latin confirmātiō. Accent on the ó marks the stressed final syllable.

mágico.etymology_derivation: Greek magikos → Latin magicus → mágico. All words in -ico carry an antepenultimate accent.

hecho.english_meaning: done, made (participle of hacer); fact (el hecho)
hecho.shift_rule: Double sound shift: factum → hecho (f→h AND ct→ch!)
hecho.etymology_derivation: Look at Latin factum → Spanish hecho: initial f- became silent h-, AND medial -ct- became -ch-!

lleno.etymology_derivation: Latin plēnus ('full', English plenty/replenish) shifted initial pl- to ll-: lleno!

gustar.english_meaning: to be pleasing to (me gusta: I like, lit. it pleases to me)
gustar.shift_rule: Inverted dative experiencer verb (gusta sg. / gustan pl.)
gustar.context_phrase: Me gusta el café y me gustan los libros.
gustar.context_translation: I like coffee and I like books.
gustar.etymology_derivation: Latin gustāre ('to taste') — English gusto and disgust. The thing liked is the grammatical SUBJECT!

gustaría.english_cognate: would please (me gustaría: I would like)
gustaría.english_meaning: would please (conditional: me gustaría = I would like)
gustaría.context_translation: I would like to reserve a table.
gustaría.etymology_derivation: Every Spanish conditional simply glues -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían onto the whole infinitive!

conocer.english_meaning: to know, be familiar with (people, places; conozco: I know)
conocer.shift_rule: 1st sg in -zco: conozco (takes personal 'a' before people!)
conocer.context_phrase: Conozco Madrid y conozco a tu hermano.
conocer.context_translation: I know Madrid and I know your brother.
conocer.etymology_derivation: Before a specific person, conhecer ALWAYS requires the personal 'a': conozco a María!

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
